ghetto-house.d: Chicago house's most feral strain: 808 drum machines, explicit shouted vocals and minimal loops; DJ Deeon and the Dance Mania label are underground legends.

ballroom.d: The soundtrack to New York's Black and Latinx queer ballroom culture: hard house beats plus vogue dancing; Masters at Work's 'The Ha Dance' is the anthem.

afro-tech.d: Swaps afro-house's drum kits for colder, more hypnotic synths and low end; Black Coffee carried it to the rest of the world.

organic-house.d: House made slower and more 'organic': hand percussion, acoustic samples and long gradual builds; Keinemusik is the face of this wave.

lo-fi-house.d: House run through tape and samplers, then smeared with noise: nostalgic, rough and bedroom-made; Ross from Friends is the exemplar.

ambient-techno.d: Techno's skeleton soaked in synth pads: still danceable, but closer to drifting; Aphex Twin's 'Xtal' is the template.

ghettotech.d: Where Detroit meets Chicago: techno tempo, electro drum machines and foul-mouthed shouting; DJ Assault is the figurehead.

future-garage.d: 2-step garage smashed into fragments and reassembled: vocal chops, rain sounds, sub bass and negative space; Burial's album of the same name defined it.

gqom.d: Durban's minimal bass music: just a kick, claps and one bleak synth line, emptier and meaner than house.

uk-funky.d: A short-lived late-2000s London scene: house beats plus soca and African drums; Crazy Cousinz pushed it onto radio.

memphis-rap.d: Lo-fi drum machines, eerie synths and underground tape releases; Three 6 Mafia turned Memphis's horror into DNA for later trap and phonk.

alternative-hip-hop.d: Hip-hop that refuses the gangsta path: oddball samples, and themes introspective or irreverent; De La Soul's '3 Feet High and Rising' opened the door.

political-hip-hop.d: The microphone used as a flyer: race, police and power structures; Public Enemy's 'Fight the Power' is the loudest note.

instrumental-hip-hop.d: Hip-hop without vocals: samples and drum kits treated as composition; DJ Shadow's 'Endtroducing.....' made it a complete album art form.

hyphy.d: The Bay Area's party rap: fast hi-hats, synth leads and 'go dumb' dance culture; E-40 is the godfather.

snap.d: Southern party rap built on finger snaps and 808s; Lil Jon's shouting carried it up the 2000s charts.

mumble-rap.d: A generation of rap where diction gives way to melody and atmosphere: timbre and groove matter more than lyrics; Future is its biggest influence.

soundcloud-rap.d: The next generation of rap, recorded in bedrooms and uploaded direct: lo-fi, emotional and genre-blurring; Lil Uzi Vert and XXXTentacion went from the platform to the charts.

emo-rap.d: Emo's self-harm narratives and guitar samples fed into trap drums; Lil Peep and XXXTentacion let two subcultures meet on the same playlist.

trap-soul.d: R&B melodies sung over trap's 808s and hi-hats; Bryson Tiller's 'T R A P S O U L' gave the wave its name.

uk-drill.d: Chicago drill reborn in London: sliding 808s, cold melodies and block narrative, forming Britain's sharpest generation of rap.

afroswing.d: London's young African diaspora wired afrobeats melody to grime rhythm; J Hus is the loudest name of this wave.

latin-rap.d: US Latin rap switching between Spanish and English; Kid Frost's 'La Raza' is the starting point of West Coast Latin rap.

phonk.d: An internet subspecies grown from Memphis rap samples: distorted 808s, cowbells and lo-fi haze, later splitting off into drift phonk.
